title: Merge Two Sorted Arrays
directAnswer: Merge with two pointers: compare `a[i]` and `b[j]`, append the smaller, advance that pointer. When one runs out, append the rest of the other. O(n+m).

remember.takeaway: Merging sorted inputs is linear — never re-sort.
remember.formula: while i<n and j<m: out += smaller(a[i],b[j]); advance; then drain
whenToUse: Merge step of merge sort / k-way merge
antiSignals: Inputs unsorted — sort first or use a different method

problemStatement: Given two arrays `a` and `b`, each sorted in non-decreasing order, return a single sorted array containing all their elements.
understanding: Two pointers walk both arrays, always copying the smaller current element first.

approaches.name: Two-pointer merge
approaches.whenToMention: This is the standard, expected solution — lead with it.
approaches.explanation:
Because both inputs are already sorted, you can merge them in linear time with **two pointers**: repeatedly take the smaller of the two current fronts and advance that pointer. This is the merge step of merge sort.

**Why it's linear, not n log n.** Re-concatenating and sorting throws away the sortedness you already have and costs O((n+m)log(n+m)). The two-pointer merge exploits the existing order — each element is emitted exactly once, so it's O(n+m).

**Why advance only the consumed pointer.** You output one element per step (the smaller front) and move only that array's pointer; the other front is still the smallest unprocessed value on its side, ready for the next comparison.

**Stability and leftovers.** Use `a[i] <= b[j]` (not `<`) so equal elements keep a's-before-b's order and none are dropped. When one array empties, append the entire remainder of the other — that tail is already sorted.
hints: Both arrays are sorted — what's the cheapest way to combine them?
Compare the two front elements; take the smaller and advance that pointer.
When one runs out, append the rest of the other.
approaches.insight: Re-sorting the concatenation is O((n+m)log(n+m)); the linear merge exploits the existing sortedness.
approaches.complexityReasoning: each of the n+m elements is emitted once with O(1) work; the output array is O(n+m) space.

java.explanation: Append the smaller front and advance only that pointer.
Drain whichever array still has elements.

edgeCases.behavior: One side empty — just copy the other.
No interleave needed; a then b.

pitfalls: Forgetting to copy the leftovers after one pointer is exhausted.
Using `<` instead of `<=` and dropping or reordering equal elements.

commonMistakes: Forgetting to copy the leftovers after one pointer is exhausted.
Using `<` instead of `<=` and dropping/duplicating equal elements (stability).

clarifyingQuestions.question: Are both inputs guaranteed sorted?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: Yes — that's what makes the linear merge valid.
